rectifier.title: Rectifiers: Diode and Thyristor AC-DC Conversion
rectifier.intro: The Rectifier studio converts a sinusoidal supply into a unidirectional load voltage and reports the quantities that define converter quality: average output, RMS output, form factor and ripple factor.
rectifier.purpose: This tool simulates single-phase and three-phase rectifiers, from uncontrolled diode circuits (firing angle $\alpha = 0^\circ$) to phase-controlled thyristor (SCR) converters. It draws the source, the output voltage and the load current on the scope for resistive, inductive, capacitive and back-EMF loads, with or without a freewheeling diode, and computes $V_{dc}$, $V_{rms}$, $FF$, $RF$, power factor and efficiency from the sampled waveforms.

model.heading: Average output voltage
model.body: For a single-phase fully-controlled bridge with continuous conduction (a highly inductive load that keeps the current non-zero), the average output is $V_{dc} = \frac{2V_m}{\pi}\cos\alpha$. Setting $\alpha = 0^\circ$ gives the diode bridge value $\frac{2V_m}{\pi}$, and $\alpha > 90^\circ$ makes $V_{dc}$ negative, which is inverter-mode operation when the load supplies energy (for example a back-EMF source). A resistive load enters discontinuous conduction and gives $V_{dc} = \frac{V_m}{\pi}(1 + \cos\alpha)$ instead.

model.heading: RMS value, form factor and ripple factor
model.body: With continuous conduction the output waveform is a rectified, shifted sine whose RMS value stays $V_{rms} = \frac{V_m}{\sqrt{2}}$ for every $\alpha$, so only the average moves. The form factor is $FF = V_{rms}/V_{dc}$ and the ripple factor $RF = \sqrt{(V_{rms}/V_{dc})^2 - 1}$ measures the AC content relative to the DC content. Both grow quickly as $\alpha$ approaches $90^\circ$ because $V_{dc}$ shrinks while $V_{rms}$ does not.

model.heading: Three-phase bridge
model.body: The six-pulse bridge with peak phase voltage $V_m$ gives $V_{dc} = \frac{3\sqrt{3}\,V_m}{\pi}\cos\alpha$ under continuous conduction, and the output ripple frequency rises to $6f$. The higher pulse number gives a much lower $RF$ than the single-phase circuit and needs far less filtering.

model.heading: Freewheeling diode and commutation
model.body: With an inductive load, the output voltage would go negative once the supply reverses. A freewheeling diode clamps the output to zero at that moment and carries the load current, so the thyristors turn off naturally and $V_{dc}$ follows $\frac{V_m}{\pi}(1 + \cos\alpha)$. Source inductance $L_s$ delays current transfer between devices by an overlap angle $\mu$, described by $\cos\alpha - \cos(\alpha + \mu) = \frac{2\omega L_s I_d}{V_m}$, and removes the average voltage $\Delta V_{dc} = \frac{2\omega L_s}{\pi} I_d$.

equations: Average DC output of the single-phase fully-controlled bridge, continuous conduction.
RMS output voltage under continuous conduction, independent of the firing angle.
Form factor: ratio of RMS to average output voltage.
Ripple factor derived from the form factor.
Average output with a freewheeling diode or a resistive load.
Average output of the three-phase six-pulse controlled bridge.
Commutation overlap angle caused by the source inductance.
Average voltage drop due to commutation overlap.

mapping.body: Selects between the single-phase relations with $2V_m/\pi$ and the three-phase relation with $3\sqrt{3}V_m/\pi$, and sets the pulse number of the output.
Half-wave, full-wave bridge or center-tapped. Half-wave has a single pulse per cycle, so its average is $V_m/\pi$ at $\alpha = 0^\circ$; the full-wave circuits double the pulse count.
The input is read either as an RMS value or as the peak $V_m$. Internally $V_m = \sqrt{2}\,V_{RMS}$ is used in every formula.
The supply frequency sets $\omega = 2\pi f$, shown in the panel, and the period of the scope. It also scales the overlap term $\omega L_s$.
The thyristor firing delay. At $\alpha = 0^\circ$ the circuit behaves as a diode rectifier; the metric $V_{DC}$ follows $\cos\alpha$.

mapping.term: Load Type (R, RL, RC, RLC, RLE)
mapping.body: Chooses which of $R$, $L$, $C$ and $E$ are active. Inductance gives continuous current, capacitance gives a peak-charging waveform with large ripple, and $E$ creates a conduction blocking threshold.
Available for inductive loads. Switching it on clamps negative output segments and replaces the continuous-conduction formula with the $(1 + \cos\alpha)$ form.
Displays $V_{RMS}$, $V_{DC}$, $I_{RMS}$, $I_{DC}$, $P_{DC}$, $P_{AC}$, $V_{ripple}$, $FF$, $RF$, $PF$ and $\eta$, all computed from the waveform samples.

example.title: Single-phase controlled bridge, highly inductive load
example.problem: A single-phase fully-controlled bridge is fed with a peak voltage $V_m = 100\text{ V}$, fires at $\alpha = 60^\circ$ and supplies a load of $R = 10\text{ }\Omega$ whose inductance keeps the current continuous. Find the output quality figures.

steps.text: Compute the average output voltage from the continuous-conduction formula.
The RMS value does not depend on $\alpha$ in continuous conduction.
Form factor from the two voltages.
Ripple factor from the form factor.
Average load current and DC power, using $I_{dc} = V_{dc}/R$.

example.result: $V_{dc} = 31.83\text{ V}$, $V_{rms} = 70.71\text{ V}$, $FF = 2.221$ and $RF = 1.984$. Raising $\alpha$ toward $90^\circ$ drives $V_{dc}$ to zero and the ripple factor to infinity, which is why the converter is used with a filter or a freewheeling path.

applications.body: Phase-controlled bridges regulate armature voltage in rolling mills, cranes and machine-tool spindles, and inverter mode allows regenerative braking.
Controlled rectifiers supply adjustable DC to chargers, electroplating and electrochemical plants, where the average current must be tuned precisely.
Large three-phase thyristor bridges convert at transmission level, with commutation overlap setting the voltage regulation of the link.
Phase control sets the output energy of resistance welders and induction furnace supplies from the same three-phase source.

inverter.title: Inverters: Single-Phase and Three-Phase Voltage Source Inverters
inverter.intro: The Inverter studio synthesizes an AC waveform from a DC bus using switch gating patterns and measures the fundamental amplitude and the harmonic distortion of the result.
inverter.purpose: This tool simulates a single-phase half-bridge or full-bridge inverter and a three-phase six-switch voltage source inverter with $180^\circ$ or $120^\circ$ conduction. The switching technique can be square wave, single-pulse, multi-pulse or sinusoidal PWM (SPWM). The scope shows the gate pattern, the pole and load voltages and the load current, and the metrics report $V_1$, $THD$, power factor and power.

model.heading: Sinusoidal PWM definitions
model.body: SPWM compares a sinusoidal control signal with a triangular carrier. The amplitude modulation index is $m_a = V_{control}/V_{tri}$ and the frequency modulation ratio is $m_f = f_s/f_1$, where $f_s$ is the carrier frequency and $f_1$ the fundamental. The linear range is $m_a \le 1$; beyond it the converter enters overmodulation and approaches a square wave.

model.heading: Fundamental voltage
model.body: For a full-bridge with bipolar switching in the linear range, the fundamental RMS voltage is $V_{1,rms} = \frac{m_a V_{dc}}{\sqrt{2}}$. A half-bridge produces only $\pm V_{dc}/2$, so its fundamental is halved. A square-wave full bridge gives $V_{1,rms} = \frac{4V_{dc}}{\pi\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.9V_{dc}$.

model.heading: Six-step operation and harmonics
model.body: The three-phase six-step inverter gives a line-to-line fundamental $V_{LL,1,rms} = \frac{\sqrt{6}}{\pi}V_{dc}$ and contains only harmonics of order $6k \pm 1$. The distortion is $THD = \frac{\sqrt{\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}V_n^2}}{V_1}\times 100\%$. PWM moves the harmonics to sidebands around $m_f$ and its multiples, where a small filter can remove them.

model.heading: Dead time and shoot-through
model.body: The two switches of a leg must never conduct together, because the DC bus would be shorted. A blanking interval $t_d \ge t_{off,max} - t_{on,min}$ is inserted at every transition. It causes a voltage error of about $|\Delta V_{pole}| \approx V_{dc}t_d f_s$ per leg and adds low-order harmonics, so $t_d$ is kept as short as the devices allow.

equations: Amplitude modulation index of SPWM.
Frequency modulation ratio of SPWM.
Fundamental RMS voltage of a full-bridge in the linear range, $m_a \le 1$.
Total harmonic distortion of the output voltage.
Fundamental RMS voltage of the square-wave full-bridge.
Line-to-line fundamental RMS voltage of the three-phase six-step inverter.
Dead-time constraint to avoid shoot-through.
Approximate pole voltage error caused by dead time.

mapping.body: Switches between the single-phase bridge and the three-leg bridge with its $120^\circ$-shifted pole voltages.
Half-bridge swings $\pm V_{dc}/2$ while the full-bridge swings $\pm V_{dc}$, so the fundamental of the half-bridge is half as large.
Selects how long each switch conducts. The $180^\circ$ mode gives the standard six-step line voltage; the $120^\circ$ mode leaves one phase floating at any instant.
Square, Single-P, Multi-P or SPWM. Square has a fixed $V_1$ and $THD$; the pulse-based modes trade harmonics through the pulse width, and SPWM uses $m_a$ and $m_f$.
The output frequency $f_o$ is the fundamental $f_1$; the carrier $f_c$ is the switching frequency $f_s$ and exists only in PWM modes, so $m_f = f_c/f_o$.
Sets $m_a$. Values up to $1$ give a proportional fundamental; above $1$ the waveform saturates and the $THD$ climbs.
$V_{dc}$ scales every output. The load $R$, $RL$ or $RLE$ shapes the current, and the protection test exercises a shoot-through fault to show why dead time is required.
Reports $V_{RMS}$, $V_1$, $I_{RMS}$, $I_1$, $THD_v$, $THD_i$, $DF$, $HF$, $P$, $S$ and $PF$.

example.title: Full-bridge SPWM inverter design check
example.problem: A single-phase full-bridge inverter runs from $V_{dc} = 400\text{ V}$ with $m_a = 0.8$, a carrier $f_s = 2.5\text{ kHz}$ and an output $f_1 = 50\text{ Hz}$. The gate driver uses a dead time $t_d = 2\text{ }\mu\text{s}$. Evaluate the design.

steps.text: The modulation index is below unity, so the linear formula applies. Compute the fundamental RMS voltage.
Estimate the pole voltage error due to dead time.
Compare with the square-wave operation of the same bridge, which has a larger fundamental but poor quality.

example.result: The SPWM output has $m_f = 50$ and $V_{1,rms} = 226.3\text{ V}$, with dead-time error of about $2\text{ V}$ per leg. The square wave gives a higher $360\text{ V}$ but $THD = 48.3\%$, while SPWM pushes its harmonics near $2.5\text{ kHz}$ where a small LC filter removes them.

applications.body: Three-phase SPWM inverters control speed and torque of induction and permanent-magnet motors in robots, conveyors and machine tools.
Grid-tied inverters turn the DC link into sinusoidal current with low $THD$ to meet grid-code limits.
Full-bridge inverters rebuild the AC bus from batteries for data centers and critical manufacturing lines.
Compact inverters feed traction motors and aircraft actuators, where dead time and switching loss decide efficiency.

acvc.title: AC Voltage Controller: Phase and Integral-Cycle Control
acvc.intro: The AC Voltage Controller studio regulates the RMS voltage applied to a load by chopping the AC supply directly with thyristors, without any DC stage or frequency change.
acvc.purpose: This tool models a single-phase or three-phase AC regulator built from antiparallel thyristors or a bidirectional TRIAC. It supports phase-angle control and integral-cycle control with resistive or inductive loads, and shows the source voltage, load voltage, load current, gate pulses and conduction angles, together with $V_{o,rms}$, power factor and harmonic distortion.

model.heading: Phase-angle control, resistive load
model.body: A thyristor pair is fired at the angle $\alpha$ in each half-cycle, so the load sees the supply only from $\alpha$ to $\pi$. For a resistive load the output RMS voltage is $V_{rms} = V_s\sqrt{\frac{1}{\pi}\left(\pi - \alpha + \frac{\sin 2\alpha}{2}\right)}$ with $V_s$ the RMS supply voltage and $0 \le \alpha \le \pi$. The input power factor equals the same square root, so $PF$ falls as $\alpha$ increases.

model.heading: Inductive load
model.body: With a load angle $\varphi$ the current continues after the supply voltage crosses zero until the extinction angle $\beta$, found from $\sin(\beta - \varphi) = \sin(\alpha - \varphi)e^{-(\beta - \alpha)/\tan\varphi}$. The conduction angle is $\gamma = \beta - \alpha$. Control exists only for $\alpha \ge \varphi$; for $\alpha < \varphi$ the output is the full sine and the controller loses authority.

model.heading: Integral-cycle control
model.body: Instead of cutting each cycle, whole cycles are passed or blocked: $n_{ON}$ cycles on and $m_{OFF}$ cycles off. The duty ratio is $k = n_{ON}/(n_{ON} + m_{OFF})$ and $V_{rms} = V_s\sqrt{k}$. Switching occurs at zero crossings, so the method gives no steep current edges and no radio interference, but it produces subharmonic flicker and suits only slow thermal loads.

model.heading: Harmonic current
model.body: Phase control creates odd harmonics of the load current. For a resistive load the fundamental has coefficients $b_1 = \frac{V_m}{\pi R}\left(\pi - \alpha + \frac{\sin 2\alpha}{2}\right)$ and $a_1 = -\frac{V_m}{\pi R}\sin^2\alpha$, and the lagging component $a_1$ makes the supply current displaced even for a resistive load. A unidirectional circuit also injects a DC component and even harmonics.

equations: RMS output voltage of the single-phase phase-angle controller with resistive load.
Input power factor for the same circuit.
RMS output voltage of integral-cycle control.
Extinction angle of an inductive load.
Fourier coefficients of the fundamental load current, resistive load.
Active and apparent power of the load.

mapping.body: Chooses the single-phase circuit or a three-phase controller as a star connection with three wires, a star connection with four wires, or a delta connection, each with its own conduction intervals.
A unidirectional circuit conducts only one half-cycle and adds DC and even harmonics; the bidirectional or TRIAC circuit is symmetrical and has only odd harmonics.
Phase-Angle uses $\alpha$; Integral-Cycle uses $n_{ON}$ and $m_{OFF}$ and reports the ratio $k$.
The firing angle in the formulas above. The metrics also show the extinction angle $\beta$ and conduction angle $\gamma$.
Number of conducting and blocked supply cycles in one control period, which give $k$ and $V_{rms} = V_s\sqrt{k}$.
The supply RMS voltage or peak (selected by the voltage format) and frequency; $f$ sets the time axis of the scope.
$L$ in millihenry sets $\varphi = \arctan(\omega L/R)$ and with it $\beta$.
Optionally draws the thyristor voltage or the gate pulses on the scope so that turn-on and turn-off instants can be seen.

example.title: Resistive load at a firing angle of sixty degrees
example.problem: A single-phase bidirectional controller is fed from $V_s = 230\text{ V}$ and supplies $R = 10\text{ }\Omega$ with phase control at $\alpha = 60^\circ$. Calculate the output voltage, power and power factor.

steps.text: Evaluate the bracket in radians, using $\alpha = \pi/3$.
Divide by $\pi$ and take the square root to obtain the voltage ratio, which is also the power factor.
Load current, active power and apparent power.
For comparison, integral-cycle control with $n_{ON} = 3$ and $m_{OFF} = 1$ gives a ratio $k = 3/4 = 0.75$.

example.result: At $\alpha = 60^\circ$ the controller delivers $V_{rms} = 206.3\text{ V}$ and $P = 4256\text{ W}$ with $PF = 0.897$ (check: $P/S = 4256/4745 = 0.897$). Integral-cycle control reaches a similar voltage with unity displacement but with cycle-skipping.

applications.body: Dimmers and electric furnaces use phase control; slow thermal loads also allow integral-cycle control without interference.
Three-phase controllers ramp the stator voltage to limit starting current and mechanical shock on pumps, fans and conveyors.
Zero-crossing triggering keeps harmonic emission within grid limits for large resistive heater banks.
AC regulators stabilize line voltage for sensitive laboratory and process equipment without moving parts.

chopper.title: Choppers: Buck, Boost and Buck-Boost DC-DC Converters
chopper.intro: The Chopper studio converts a fixed DC input into a different DC output level by switching a transistor with duty cycle $D$ and smoothing the result with an inductor and a capacitor.
chopper.purpose: This tool simulates the three basic non-isolated DC-DC topologies, selected by the Buck, Boost and Buck-Boost modes, and the chopper classes A to E for one-, two- and four-quadrant operation. The scope shows the switch signal, inductor current and output voltage under PWM or frequency-modulation control and the metrics report $V_{dc}$, ripple current, $L_c$, power and efficiency.

model.heading: Buck converter
model.body: In continuous conduction the buck steps the voltage down with $V_o/V_{in} = D$. The inductor current ripple is $\Delta I_L = \frac{(V_{in} - V_o)D}{f_s L}$, and the boundary of continuous conduction is the critical inductance $L_{crit} = \frac{(1 - D)R}{2f_s}$. For $L < L_{crit}$ the current reaches zero (discontinuous conduction, DCM) and the gain rises above $D$, following $V_o/V_{in} = 2/(1 + \sqrt{1 + 4K/D^2})$ with $K = 2Lf_s/R$.

model.heading: Boost converter
model.body: The boost steps the voltage up with $V_o/V_{in} = \frac{1}{1 - D}$ in continuous conduction. The inductor current ripple is $\Delta I_L = V_{in}D/(f_s L)$ and the output capacitor supplies the load while the switch is on, giving a voltage ripple $\Delta V_o = \frac{I_o D}{f_s C}$. The critical inductance is $L_{crit} = \frac{D(1 - D)^2R}{2f_s}$, and the gain theoretically diverges as $D \to 1$ but real losses limit it.

model.heading: Buck-boost converter
model.body: The buck-boost produces an inverted output with $V_o/V_{in} = -\frac{D}{1 - D}$, so it steps down for $D < 0.5$ and up for $D > 0.5$. Its critical inductance is $L_{crit} = \frac{(1 - D)^2R}{2f_s}$ and its capacitor ripple is $\Delta V_o = I_oD/(f_s C)$. Energy is stored in the inductor during the on-time and delivered to the load during the off-time.

model.heading: CCM, DCM and control
model.body: Continuous conduction mode (CCM) holds the gain independent of the load, while DCM makes it load dependent. In pulse-width control the period is constant and $D$ varies; in frequency modulation the on-time is fixed and $f_s$ varies, so $D = t_{on}f_s$.

equations: Buck voltage gain in continuous conduction.
Buck inductor current ripple.
Buck critical inductance for the CCM/DCM boundary.
Boost voltage gain.
Boost output voltage ripple.
Buck-boost voltage gain, inverting.
Critical inductance of the boost and the buck-boost converters.
Buck gain in discontinuous conduction mode.

mapping.body: Selects the topology and with it the gain law, the ripple formula and the critical inductance.
Chooses the quadrant of operation: A and B are single-quadrant, C and D are two-quadrant and E is the four-quadrant bridge that can reverse voltage and current.
PWM changes $D$ at fixed $f_s$; frequency modulation keeps the on-time constant and varies $f_s$.
Slider and field for the duty cycle; the gain laws above are evaluated directly from it.
The switching frequency (minimum $50\text{ Hz}$) and the source voltage. Increasing $f_s$ reduces $\Delta I_L$ and $L_{crit}$.
$R$ and $L$ (in millihenry) set the ripple and whether the circuit is in CCM; $E$ models a motor back-EMF or battery.
Show the output average, current ripple, current peaks and the critical inductance in millihenry; $I_{min} > 0$ confirms CCM.
Power balance and efficiency of the simulated converter, including the switching and conduction losses of the model.

example.title: Sizing buck and boost stages at twenty kilohertz
example.problem: Both converters switch at $f_s = 20\text{ kHz}$. The buck has $V_{in} = 48\text{ V}$, $D = 0.75$, $R = 6\text{ }\Omega$ and $L = 300\text{ }\mu\text{H}$. The boost has $V_{in} = 12\text{ V}$, $D = 0.6$, $R = 15\text{ }\Omega$, $L = 100\text{ }\mu\text{H}$ and $C = 100\text{ }\mu\text{F}$. In the tool's millihenry fields, enter $0.3$ mH for the buck and $0.1$ mH for the boost. Find outputs, ripple and operating mode.

steps.text: Buck output voltage and load current.
Buck inductor ripple and current extremes.
steps.tex: \Delta I_L = \frac{(48 - 36)\times 0.75}{20000 \times 300\times 10^{-6}} = \frac{9}{6} = 1.5\text{ A}, \quad I_{max} = 6.75\text{ A}, \; I_{min} = 5.25\text{ A}

steps.text: Buck critical inductance, confirming CCM since $L$ exceeds it.
Boost output voltage and current, then capacitor ripple.
steps.tex: V_o = \frac{12}{1 - 0.6} = 30\text{ V}, \quad I_o = \frac{30}{15} = 2\text{ A}, \quad \Delta V_o = \frac{2 \times 0.6}{20000 \times 100\times 10^{-6}} = 0.6\text{ V}

steps.text: Boost critical inductance: $L = 100\,\mu\text{H}$ is above $36\,\mu\text{H}$, so the boost operates in CCM. The buck-boost output for the same $V_{in}$ and $D$ is shown for comparison.

example.result: The buck delivers $36\text{ V}$ at $6\text{ A}$ with $\Delta I_L = 1.5\text{ A}$ in CCM, and the boost delivers $30\text{ V}$ at $2\text{ A}$ with $\Delta V_o = 0.6\text{ V}$. The boost is in CCM because its inductor exceeds the $36\,\mu\text{H}$ critical value. The buck-boost would output $-18\text{ V}$ from the same source.

applications.body: Buck converters step a pack voltage down to logic and motor rails with high efficiency.
Boost stages raise the low panel voltage to the DC link and track the maximum power point through $D$.
Class C, D and E choppers move energy in both directions between the battery and the motor during braking.
Buck-boost converters keep a regulated rail while the input varies above and below the output level.
